summary: All 16 units were read in full. Every numeric key, worked example and marking-guide figure was recomputed independently in Python (APF and density, Arrhenius vacancy and diffusion values, erf case depths, true/engineering conversions, resilience and toughness, E-G-nu-K relations, Brinell/Vickers, Hall-Petch, lever-rule and Fe-C fractions, Jominy and tempering interpolations, snap-fit strain, rule of mixtures, tie masses and Ashby indices); all agree with the keys within the stated tolerances. The standard definitions and diagram statements checked (edge/screw motion, eutectic/peritectic/eutectoid, Fe-Fe3C points, martensite, Considere, tension/compression in ceramics, beam and panel indices E^(1/2)/rho and E^(1/3)/rho, snap-fit strain 3hy/(2L^2) re-derived from beam theory) are correct. Scans for control or tab characters, literal \uXXXX text, [object Object], placeholder steps and non-Latin characters were clean. No critical or major problems were found; only small precision, consistency and labelling issues remain. This is an AI review only: the course still needs a subject-matter expert before engineering reliance.

issues.problem: Hook: "A steel bar heated through 912 degrees C suddenly shrinks in length". 912 C is the BCC-to-FCC transformation of pure iron; steels transform at carbon-dependent temperatures (starting at 727 C for the eutectoid), and the contraction applies to the iron, not generally to a steel at 912 C.
issues.suggestedFix: Say "A bar of pure iron heated through 912 degrees C" (or a steel heated through its transformation range, which depends on carbon content).

issues.problem: The conduction text says that in "an ionic or covalent solid ... the nearest empty states lie across an energy gap of several eV", but the bond table lists covalent Si as "insulating or semiconducting" (gap about 1.1 eV). The covalent bond-energy range "300 to 700" kJ/mol also sits awkwardly with SiC, listed as an example (about 1200 kJ/mol in common tables).
issues.suggestedFix: State that ionic solids and many covalent ceramics have gaps of several eV, while covalent semiconductors such as Si have about 1 eV and conduct slightly at room temperature. Widen the covalent range to about 300 to 1200 kJ/mol or drop SiC from the examples.

issues.problem: "Toughness" is defined here as the area under the stress-strain curve (J/m^3). The polymers-ceramics-overview module later uses "fracture toughness" K_Ic (MPa sqrt(m)). The unit never warns that these are different quantities, so students can conflate them.
issues.suggestedFix: Add one sentence, for example in the warning callout, saying that this toughness is an energy-per-volume measure from a smooth tensile test and is not the fracture toughness K_Ic used for cracked components.

issues.problem: Alloy data in q005 to q007 (for example steel 420/560 MPa with fracture strain 0.22; Alloys A, B, P, Q) are invented and not labelled as illustrative or assumed, although the stem for q005 does carry the approximation.
issues.suggestedFix: Label the strength and strain values as illustrative or assumed, as is done elsewhere in the course.

issues.problem: Full anneal row: "Austenitise (about 30 to 50 degrees C above the upper critical temperature)". This is the rule for hypoeutectoid steels. Hypereutectoid steels are austenitised about 30 to 50 C above the lower critical temperature A1 (not above Acm) to avoid a continuous cementite network.
issues.suggestedFix: Add "hypoeutectoid steels; for hypereutectoid steels about 30 to 50 degrees C above A1", or say "above the relevant critical temperature".

issues.problem: Jominy data for Steels C and D (q004, q006) are invented and not labelled illustrative, unlike the lesson table, which is labelled.

Marking guide: "At 80 degrees C, A is within about 25 degrees C of Tg, so it is softening and prone to creep". An amorphous polymer 25 C below Tg is still essentially glassy; the modulus drop is concentrated near and above Tg, and the lesson itself puts the transition at 10 to 20 C wide. The conclusion (B preferable, check creep) stands, but the stated reason is overstated.
issues.suggestedFix: Reword to say A has a small margin below Tg, so modulus and creep resistance are already degrading and there is little safety margin for temperature excursions or long-term stress relaxation, while B has a large margin.

issues.problem: Marking guide gives the transverse (isostress) modulus as "about 9 GPa". For V_f=0.65, E_f=240, E_m=3.0 GPa, 1/E_T = 0.65/240 + 0.35/3.0 gives E_T = 8.4 GPa.

The lesson and table state the beam (E^(1/2)/rho) and panel (E^(1/3)/rho) indices and the callout in the charts unit gives slopes 2 and 3, but neither derivation is shown and no question tests them. The indices are correct (checked: fixed-shape beam I proportional to A^2 gives m proportional to rho/E^(1/2); panel I proportional to t^3 gives rho/E^(1/3)). The objectives only cover the tie.
issues.suggestedFix: Either add a short worked derivation and one question on the beam index, or mark these rows as preview material beyond the unit objectives.
